questions.prompt: Which description best captures culture in this lesson?

options.text: Learned and shared meanings, practices, values, and ways of organizing social life.
A fixed biological trait shared by every member of a population.
A single official rulebook that all members interpret identically.
Any personal preference that has never been communicated to others.

questions.explanation: Culture is learned and social, but it is also diverse, changing, and contested rather than biological, perfectly uniform, or merely private.
questions.misconception: Culture is an unchanging essence possessed by a whole group.

questions.prompt: What is a social sanction?

options.text: A response such as approval, shame, exclusion, reward, or punishment that reinforces an expectation.
A private feeling that has no connection to other people.
A proof that a norm is morally correct.
A cultural practice that has never changed.

questions.explanation: Sanctions show how a social setting encourages or discourages conduct. A sanction can support a norm without proving that the norm is morally justified.
questions.misconception: Anything enforced by a group is automatically morally right.

questions.prompt: Which claim is descriptive rather than metaethical?

options.text: Different communities actually have different expectations about some practices.
A moral judgment is justified only relative to the standards of a culture.
No moral reason can be better supported than any competing reason.
Moral truth must always be indexed to group membership.

questions.explanation: The first option reports a social fact about differences. The other options make stronger claims about what moral truth or justification is.
questions.misconception: Evidence of disagreement immediately proves moral relativism.

questions.prompt: What is ethnocentrism?

options.text: Treating one’s own cultural standards as the default measure of other groups.
Learning how a practice is understood by people who participate in it.
Recognizing disagreement within one’s own community.
Applying one rule to every case without considering context.

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism makes the familiar seem neutral and can turn difference into deficiency before the observer has learned the relevant context.
questions.misconception: Any moral criticism of a practice is ethnocentric.
questions.originality_note: Newly authored for Aralivo; not copied from a source or reviewer bank.

questions.prompt: Why does internal diversity matter to moral analysis?

options.text: It prevents us from treating a group as if every member shares one voice or practice.
It proves that groups have no norms at all.
It means outsiders can never understand any practice.
It makes power differences irrelevant within the group.

questions.explanation: Groups can have shared patterns while still containing disagreement, subcultures, unequal power, and people who resist or reinterpret a norm.
questions.misconception: Acknowledging diversity means denying that culture shapes behavior.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes moral pluralism?

options.text: More than one moral value may be genuine and relevant, even when values conflict.
Every preference is equally justified if someone wants it.
Only one culture can possess moral values.

questions.explanation: Pluralism recognizes multiple values and difficult trade-offs. It does not say that every preference is moral or that every choice is equally defensible.

questions.prompt: Why is context not the same as automatic approval?

options.text: Context explains meanings and conditions, while justification still asks about reasons, effects, and fairness.

questions.explanation: Context makes interpretation and criticism more accurate. It does not end questions about serious harm, coercion, exclusion, or unfair burden.
questions.misconception: A culturally responsive approach must either approve or remain silent.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures situated moral agency?

questions.explanation: A fair judgment considers pressure, dependence, knowledge, control, and alternatives while recognizing that people can reflect, resist, negotiate, and repair.

questions.prompt: A student says, “Our family expects adult children to help with household care, so asking for help is always morally required.” Which response is most careful?
questions.scenario: The student’s sibling is balancing work, study, disability, and caregiving. The family norm values loyalty, but the sibling says the schedule is unsafe and no one else is sharing the burden.

options.text: Respect the value of loyalty, then examine consent, capacity, burden-sharing, safety, and alternatives.
Reject family obligation because individual freedom always outweighs care.
Accept the demand because any family tradition is morally decisive.
Assume the sibling is selfish because refusal violates a familiar role.

questions.explanation: A careful judgment takes the cultural value of care seriously while asking whether the demand is safe, voluntary, fairly shared, and responsive to the person’s situation.
questions.misconception: Respecting a value requires accepting every way a family enforces it.

questions.prompt: A student moderator sees that a class group treats jokes about a minority as normal banter. What is the best first move in a culture-sensitive response?
questions.scenario: The jokes are defended as tradition, but several members stop participating and one person reports being targeted. The moderator has authority to set group rules.

options.text: Learn the context and affected members’ experiences, then address the harm and set a proportionate rule.
Leave the jokes untouched because the group calls them traditional.
Delete every informal message without checking what happened.
Ask only the most senior members whether anyone was harmed.

questions.explanation: The moderator should avoid both automatic deference and impulsive erasure: listen to those affected, identify harm and power, and use a fair rule that protects participation.
questions.misconception: A practice is harmless if its regular participants say it is only a joke.

questions.prompt: A group argues that a workplace practice is fair because “everyone here has always done it.” Which analysis is strongest?
questions.scenario: The practice assigns late shifts mostly to workers with less seniority, who cannot easily refuse because schedules affect their income. Senior workers describe the arrangement as respectful tradition.

options.text: Investigate the history and value of the practice, then assess whether the burden and limited refusal power are fair.
Accept it because repetition proves the practice is morally correct.
Reject every tradition as an obstacle to fairness.
Ignore the junior workers because senior workers define the culture.

questions.explanation: The best analysis respects context while making burden, income dependence, and refusal power visible. Tradition explains a practice; it does not settle fairness.
questions.misconception: A practice cannot be criticized if it has a history of acceptance.
